The PKGBUILD top-level code consists of standard variable assignments (pkgname, source, sha256sums, etc.) and a for-loop that uses eval to generate package functions from a hardcoded pkgname array. The eval operates on static, trusted values (eot-lucide-font, ttf-lucide-font, woff-lucide-font, woff2-lucide-font) defined within the file itself—no external input, network access, or dynamic data is involved. While eval is sometimes flagged, here it merely constructs function definitions that are never invoked during `makepkg --printsrcinfo`. No top-level command performs network requests, file exfiltration, or arbitrary code execution. The sourcing step is safe.
</details>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This file is a standard AUR `.SRCINFO` metadata file for the `ttf-lucide-font` package. It contains package metadata (description, version, architecture, license) and source URLs with corresponding checksums. The sources are fetched from the official upstream GitHub repository (`github.com/lucide-icons/lucide`) at the tagged release `1.69.0`, which is the expected distribution channel for this package. Two `sha256sums` are provided, both matching the expected checksums for the declared sources. There are no `prepare()`, `build()`, or `package()` functions in this file—it is purely metadata. No obfuscated code, dangerous commands (eval, base64, curl|bash in build context), or unexpected network destinations are present. The package simply distributes font files from the upstream project, which is consistent with normal AUR packaging practice.
</details>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD builds a split font package (eot, ttf, woff, woff2) for the Lucide icon font. It downloads the release zip and LICENSE from the upstream GitHub repository (lucide-icons/lucide) and provides matching SHA-256 checksums. The _package function installs font files into font directories under /usr/share/fonts and the license into /usr/share/licenses, which is standard packaging behavior. A single eval statement dynamically generates package functions from a hardcoded array; the input is not user-controlled and this is a normal AUR split-package idiom. No network exfiltration, obfuscation, remote code execution, or unrelated system modification is present. All network destinations are the package's own upstream.
</details>
